summary: Specifies QUIC version 2, which is nearly identical to version 1. Its purpose is to fight ossification by middleboxes and to exercise the version negotiation mechanism. It also serves as a template for minimal changes in future versions.

plainLanguage.summary: It is nearly the same game with a few small rule tweaks, made so that nobody gets stuck assuming the rules can never change.

questions: what is the quic version 2 version number
subtitle: A near-copy of QUIC version 1 with a few changed constants, made to keep middleboxes from freezing the protocol in place.

tldr.problem: If nearly all QUIC traffic uses version 1, middleboxes may come to depend on the version bytes, the Initial packet key derivation and the packet formats, which would make future changes hard.
tldr.mechanism: QUIC version 2 is identical to version 1 except for a new version number, different Long Header packet type bits, a new Initial salt, new HKDF labels and a new Retry Integrity Tag key and nonce.
tldr.outcome: It exercises the version negotiation framework, provides some protection against ossification, and serves as a template for the minimum changes in any future QUIC version.

today: RFC 9369 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says version 2 is not intended to deprecate version 1.

sections.title: Why a Second Version Exists
sections.content:
QUIC version 1 has many extension points, including the version number in the second through fifth bytes of every long header. If experimental versions are rare and version 1 carries the vast majority of QUIC traffic, middleboxes could come to depend on the version bytes, which are usually 0x00000001.

Version 1 Initial packets are encrypted with a version-specific salt, which lets observers read their contents, including the TLS Client Hello or Server Hello. That creates the same risk that middleboxes ossify on the version 1 key derivation and packet formats.

Finally, RFC 9368 describes two ways to negotiate versions: an incompatible method that costs an extra round trip, and a compatible method that avoids it but limits how much the versions may differ. QUIC version 2 is meant to mitigate ossification and exercise these mechanisms. It also shows the minimum set of changes needed to define a new QUIC version. Any endpoint that supports two versions needs version negotiation to protect against downgrade attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone always plays with the same rulebook, some referees start to think no other rulebook exists. A second, almost identical rulebook keeps them honest.

sections.title: What Differs From Version 1
sections.content:
Except for a few differences, version 2 endpoints MUST implement version 1 as described in RFC 9000, RFC 9001 and RFC 9002. The differences are small.

  • Version field: long headers carry 0x6b3343cf, the first four bytes of the sha256sum of "QUICv2 version number". The wire value is not 2, to minimize ossification risk.
  • Long Header packet types: Initial is 0b01, 0-RTT is 0b10, Handshake is 0b11 and Retry is 0b00.
  • Initial salt: 0x0dede3def700a6db819381be6e269dcbf9bd2ed9, the first 20 bytes of the sha256sum of "QUICv2 salt".
  • HKDF labels: "quic key", "quic iv", "quic hp" and "quic ku" become "quicv2 key", "quicv2 iv", "quicv2 hp" and "quicv2 ku".
  • Retry Integrity Tag: a new key (0x8fb4b01b56ac48e260fbcbcead7ccc92) and nonce (0xd86969bc2d7c6d9990efb04a), derived from the sha256sum of "QUICv2 retry secret" with the "quicv2 key" and "quicv2 iv" labels.

The RFC says the random version number and the changed packet type bits are meant to combat ossification and are not strictly required of a new QUIC version.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same game with a new name tag, a new secret handshake and a few swapped labels. Everything else works the way it did before.

sections.title: Version Negotiation Rules
sections.content:
Version 2 is not meant to deprecate version 1. Because HTTP clients often use Alt-Svc to discover QUIC support, and that mechanism does not distinguish QUIC versions, HTTP servers SHOULD support multiple versions. Any endpoint that supports version 2 MUST send, process and validate the version_information transport parameter from RFC 9368 to prevent downgrade attacks. Versions 1 and 2 are compatible with each other, so servers can switch a connection between them with compatible negotiation, which endpoints supporting both SHOULD support to avoid a round trip.

The rules are the same in either direction:

  • A server that sends Retry MUST use the original version, and the client MUST NOT change version in the Initial packet carrying the Retry token. The server MAY encode the version in the token to check this.
  • The server MUST send all CRYPTO frames using the negotiated version. Before it can process the client's transport parameters, it answers Initial packets in the original version.
  • The client learns the negotiated version from the first long header whose Version field differs from the original, and SHOULD then send Initial packets in that version.
  • Both endpoints MUST send Handshake and 1-RTT packets in the negotiated version and MUST drop packets in any other version.
  • The client MUST NOT send 0-RTT packets in the negotiated version. Servers can accept 0-RTT and process 0-RTT packets from the original version.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides start by speaking the old way, work out which version they both like, then switch together. Nobody is allowed to sneak the wrong version in later.

sections.title: Tickets, Tokens and Applications
sections.content:
TLS session tickets and NEW_TOKEN tokens belong to the QUIC version of the connection that issued them. Clients MUST NOT use a ticket or token from a version 1 connection to start a version 2 connection, or the reverse. Servers MUST check the originating version and refuse one from a different version. A rejected ticket falls back to a full TLS handshake without 0-RTT. A rejected token leaves the client address unverified, which limits how much data the server can send. After compatible negotiation, tickets and tokens map to the negotiated version, not the original one.

Version 2 changes nothing about what applications can do. All ALPN codepoints defined for version 1 can also run over version 2, including h3 and doq, and unless stated otherwise, extensions defined for version 1 also work with version 2.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket for one version is like a ticket for one theater. You cannot use it at the other, so you just go through the regular entrance again.

sections.title: Ossification and Security
sections.content:
Version 2 protects against some forms of ossification. Devices that assume every long header encodes version 1, or that the version 1 Initial key derivation will never change, will not process version 2 packets correctly. However, many middleboxes such as firewalls focus on the first packet of a connection, which will often remain in version 1 format. A client that wants to fight middlebox ossification can start with version 2 if it is reasonably sure the server supports it and accepts a round-trip penalty if wrong. A server that issues a session ticket for version 2 signals an intent to keep supporting it while the ticket is valid.

Version 2 makes no change to the security or privacy properties of version 1. Mandatory version negotiation guards against downgrade attacks, though downgrades have no security implications because the versions have identical properties. The RFC also notes that support for version 2 can help an observer fingerprint both client and server devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching versions does not make anything safer or riskier. It just stops gatekeepers from assuming the rules are carved in stone, though it may help a watcher guess which devices are talking.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Test Samples
sections.content:
IANA added two entries to the QUIC Versions registry. The value 0x6b3343cf has status permanent. The value 0x709a50c4 has status provisional and is noted as the QUIC v2 draft codepoint.

Appendix A provides sample packet protection so implementations can be verified step by step. It uses an 8-byte client-chosen Destination Connection ID of 0x8394c8f03e515708 and includes a client Initial, a server Initial, a Retry, and a ChaCha20-Poly1305 short header packet. These samples are test data for implementers.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version number was written in an official list, and the RFC includes worked examples so builders can check that their code gets the same answers.
